params.textField: A thrombus that forms in the arterial system can break off and travel down the artery, into vessels, causing a *stroke or myocardial infarction*. If it breaks off from the venous system, it will go into the pulmonary blood flow, causing a *pulmonary embolism*. To prevent thrombi formation, we target two of the important steps in *haemostasis*, or the stoppage of blood: the platelet plug formation and the clotting cascade. Platelets are small cell fragments that do not have the ability to synthesise new products, so if they are damaged or in some way, lose one of the products they need to work most effectively, they will not be able to regain that product. Platelets are equipped with *contractile proteins* including actin and myosin. Their mitochondria produce *ADP* which causes the platelet to change shape, and they have enzymes, especially *cyclooxygenase (COX)* that synthesises pro-platelet prostaglandins.

params.textField: After the platelets begin to aggregate, the clotting cascade begins to stabilize the plug. The clotting cascade consists of a series of *proteins* that each in themselves, contribute to *haemostasis*. The cascade is often likened to dominoes that are set up to fall when the one preceding it falls. The ultimate result of the clotting cascade is an insoluble protein called *fibrin* that forms a meshwork, stabilizing the plug. Interestingly, when one of the proteins of the coagulation cascade is missing as it may be in a *genetic disorder* or affected by an *anticoagulant*, it affects the entire cascade, and there is less clotting. Fibrin is considered an insoluble protein because there needs to be a *proteolytic enzyme* to degrade the fibrin, which is achieved by a smaller cascade of events which ultimately results in plasminogen being cleaved to the proteolytic agent, plasmin.
